body.objective: Students will be able to use the four critique steps.
body.iCan: I can use the four critique steps.
successCriteria: I can describe what I see in an artwork
I can analyze how the elements of art are used
I can interpret meaning and judge an artwork with reasons
body.hook: Two people can look at the same painting and see completely different things. One sees a calm forest; another sees something lonely and dark. Neither is wrong, but the best art critics back up what they see with evidence. Today you'll learn a four-step method that turns "I like it" into a real response.

vocabulary.definition: To list what you see in an artwork without giving opinions.
To explain how the artist used the elements and principles of art.
To explain what you think the artwork means or expresses.
To give a reasoned opinion about an artwork's success.
The building blocks of art: line, shape, form, space, texture, value and colour.
A careful, structured response to an artwork.

study.title: The Four-Step Critique
study.question: How do I respond to art with evidence?
study.passage:
Step 1, Describe: What do you see? List subjects, colours, lines, shapes and materials. No opinions yet.
Step 2, Analyze: How is it organized? Where does your eye go first? Which elements stand out? How are balance, contrast and emphasis used?
Step 3, Interpret: What mood or idea does it express? What might the artist be saying? Use evidence: "The dark blues and heavy shapes make it feel..."
Step 4, Judge: Is it successful? Why? Judge by what the artist was trying to do, not only whether you like it.
Artworks to discuss (show images from a gallery website):
A. Emily Carr, a painting of a British Columbia forest (1930s): swirling greens, tall trunks, rhythmic brushstrokes.
B. Kenojuak Ashevak, The Enchanted Owl (1960): an Inuit print of an owl with feathers spreading in bold, flat shapes of red and black.
C. Alex Janvier, an artist from Cold Lake First Nations in Alberta: flowing, colourful lines and symbols connected to the land and Dene culture.
In groups, choose one artwork and complete all four steps on a critique sheet. Each group shares its interpretation and the evidence behind it.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers show images from public gallery and museum websites.

body.hook: Artists all over the world paint and carve the land, animals and seasons, but they don't all see nature the same way. A Japanese woodblock wave, an Inuit print of an owl and a Canadian forest painting each tell you something about the culture that made them.

study.title: Nature Across Cultures
study.question: How do different cultures show nature in art?
study.passage:
Artworks to compare (show images from public museum websites):
A. Katsushika Hokusai, The Great Wave off Kanagawa (Japan, about 1831): a woodblock print with a huge curling wave, small boats and Mount Fuji in the distance; flat areas of blue, strong outlines, claw-like foam.
B. Kenojuak Ashevak, The Enchanted Owl (Canada, Inuit, 1960): a stonecut print of an owl with feathers spreading outward in bold red and black shapes.
C. Emily Carr, a forest painting from the 1930s (Canada): towering trees and swirling green brushstrokes that seem to move.
Task: In pairs, choose two artworks. For each, note the subject, how nature is shown (realistic, stylized, patterned), colours, lines and what the work suggests about how the artist's culture sees nature. Complete a Venn diagram, then write a comparison paragraph using evidence.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers show images from public gallery and museum websites.

body.objective: Students will be able to respond to an Alberta artist's work.

successCriteria: I can respond to an Alberta artist's work using the four critique steps
I can connect an artwork to its time and place

body.hook: Alberta is full of artists: painters of prairie skies, Indigenous artists whose work speaks of land and memory, and sculptors whose public art you might walk past every day. Today you respond to an Alberta artist's work as a thoughtful critic.

vocabulary.definition: An artist who lives or worked in Alberta.
The time, place and situation in which an artwork was made.

study.title: Alberta Art Response
study.question: How do I respond thoughtfully to an artwork from my province?
study.passage:
Alberta artists to choose from (summaries written for this lesson; show images from gallery websites):
Alex Janvier (Denesuline and Saulteaux, born 1935, Cold Lake First Nations): known for flowing, colourful curving lines and symbols. His huge ceiling mural Morning Star (1993) is in the Canadian Museum of History. His work reflects the land, Dene culture and residential school experiences.
Illingworth Kerr (1905–1989): painted bold, colourful prairie and foothills landscapes and taught at the Alberta College of Art in Calgary.
Marion Nicoll (1909–1985): a Calgary artist and one of the first in Alberta to make abstract art, using bold shapes and colours.
Task: Choose one artwork. Complete the four critique steps (describe, analyze, interpret, judge). Then add context: When and where was it made? How might the artist's life and place shape the work? End with a personal response: one connection to your own life.
study.source: Summaries written for this lesson; teachers show images from public gallery websites such as the Art Gallery of Alberta.
steps: Write a personal response with evidence
